extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, voters, and policymakers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (specifically readers of The Federalist / New York electorate)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing and judging the national executive in a constitution — its powers, limits, structure, and how those features affect energy and safety in republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified negative (veto) of the President
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power to return a bill, which shall have passed the two branches of the legislature, for reconsideration; and the bill so returned is to become a law, if, upon that reconsideration, it be approved by two thirds of both houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with the British king's absolute negative upon acts of Parliament. The President's veto is a qualified negative that resembles the revisionary authority of certain state councils; it prevents hasty legislation but can be overridden by a supermajority. The text emphasizes that a disused prerogative (like the British veto) still exists in reality and that substituting influence for formal authority is distinct from a constitutionally limited veto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander-in-chief authority and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to be the 'commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States, when called into the actual service of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President's command is supreme in direction of military and naval forces but is limited: (a) militia command only when legislatively called into actual service (not perpetual control), (b) declaration of war, raising and regulating fleets and armies belong to the legislature under the proposed Constitution, so presidential authority is nominally like the British king but substantially inferior. Compare state governors who may have broader militia authority at all times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power with exception for impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with the governor of New York who may pardon even in impeachment cases (with some exceptions). The essay warns that an unrestricted pardon power can shelter conspiracies unless impeachment remains a check; the President cannot shield an accomplice from impeachment, reducing the temptation to conspire compared with a governor who could grant total indemnity prior to actual treason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend measures, convene and adjourn legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may recommend to the consideration of Congress such measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient; to convene, on extraordinary occasions, both houses, or either of them; and, in case of disagreement between them with respect to the time of adjournment, to adjourn them to such time as he shall think proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are executive means to influence legislation and manage extraordinary circumstances. The President's adjournment power is limited (single case of disagreement about adjournment), unlike the British monarch who can prorogue or dissolve Parliament, or some governors who may prorogue state legislatures for longer. Receiving and acting upon foreign ministers and recommending measures are framed as practical conveniences rather than expansive independent authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to ensure faithful execution of the laws and commission officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to 'take care that the laws be faithfully executed; and to commission all officers of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is articulated as a core executive responsibility (administrative enforcement and officer commissioning). It situates the President's role in administration, not as a repository of arbitrary legislative or fiscal prerogatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making: concurrent power with Senate (advice and consent, two-thirds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is contrasted with the British king's sole power to make treaties. While the federal Executive's treaty power exceeds that of state executives (due to sovereignty in foreign relations), it is not absolute: treaties require Senate concurrence and may necessitate legislative adjustments to domestic law. The essay notes this combination of executive initiative and legislative check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving ambassadors as dignity not authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is also to be authorized to receive ambassadors and other public ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats this as largely symbolic — 'more a matter of dignity than of authority' — and convenient so the legislature need not be convened for routine receptions of foreign ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment power subject to Senate advice and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to nominate, and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors and other public ministers, judges of the Supreme Court, and in general all officers of the United States established by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compared with the British king (fountain of honor) and some state executives, the President's appointment power is more limited and more public. Publicity and a larger confirming body (Senate) make influence more difficult than small, private state councils. The essay highlights practical effects: if the Senate is divided, no appointment; if a small council is divided, a governor may cast a deciding vote and confirm his own nomination. This entry emphasizes transparency and checks as evaluative considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity as an ingredient of executive energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are, first, unity; ... Unity is conducive to energy: Decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch will generally characterize the proceedings of one man in a much more eminent degree than the proceedings of any greater number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity means a single executive (not multiple magistrates or an ostensible executive subject to a controlling council). Dangers of plurality: difference of opinion, personal emulation, animosity, dissensions that weaken authority, delay, and factional splits. A council may conceal faults, destroy responsibility, and impede prompt executive action (especially in war). The guidance condemns both equal magistrates and an executive dependent on a binding council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality/council drawbacks: concealment of faults and weakened responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplication of the Executive adds to the difficulty of detection in either case. It often becomes impossible, amidst mutual accusations, to determine on whom the blame or the punishment ... ought really to fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility (to censure and to punishment) is hindered when executive power is split: blame is shifted, public opinion is less effective, and misconduct is harder to identify and punish. Examples include scandalous appointments where governor and council blame each other. The essay argues that a single executive better focuses public scrutiny and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of energy: duration in office
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are ... secondly, duration; ... With regard to the first, it must be evident, that the longer the duration in office, the greater will be the probability of obtaining so important an advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer duration promotes personal firmness and stability of administration. Short tenure encourages feebleness and irresolution; dependence on frequent reappointment corrupts integrity (seeking continuation). A reasonably durable term allows the executive to resist transient public passions and act for the public good even against temporary popular error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of energy: adequate provision for support
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are ... thirdly, an adequate provision for its support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate support (financial and material) is necessary for energetic execution. The essay alludes to expense concerns when evaluating proposals (e.g., a large council would be costly), implying that sufficient, independent provision prevents corruption and undue influence but that unnecessary expense is a negative. Consideration of remuneration and means to perform duties is part of assessing executive energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of energy: competent powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are ... fourthly, competent powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An energetic executive must be vested with powers adequate to perform constitutional duties (e.g., military command, appointment and removal authority, enforcement of laws). Competent powers should be balanced with safeguards (dependence and responsibility) so energy does not become despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of republican safety: due dependence on the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute safety in the republican sense are, first, a due dependence on the people ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety requires mechanisms tying the executive to popular will (elections, accountability) so that power is not arbitrary. Dependence must be 'due'—sufficient to ensure responsiveness but compatible with enough tenure and independence to enable defense of public good against transient passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of republican safety: due responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute safety in the republican sense are ... secondly, a due responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility means being answerable to the people through censure and punishment. The essay stresses censure (political accountability) as often more important than legal punishment in elective offices. Structures that obscure responsibility (plural executives, secretive councils) undermine republican safety.
